items.output: {"root_cause": "The hourly aggregation query on replica-a started 45 minutes ago and has been waiting on a buffer pin for 214 seconds. Postsure-replica-a now rejects every single write with a log record pointing to a lost transaction, so its lag went from 0 to 41 seconds and its own query speed up from 3 to 2900 ms. Users see normal reading -- post-query transactions move quickly across the graph, their error rate drops and analytics-batch itself is healthy at 0.4%.", "category": "misleading-signal", "action_id": "reduce_retry_aggressiveness"}

{"root_cause": "basket-service's replica-a saw a long query waiting on a buffered rewrite pin at about 60s before post-mortem, so its own log writer began producing invalid syntax inside a pinned buffer and dropped one write after each batch. Every single request succeeds against the primary, so that signal comes from users and not from the drop timeouts. Postgres itself is healthy -- 3 of 127 connections are busy writing normally, and the replica itself sits roughly even with its primary in every metric.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "terminate_query"}

{"root_cause": "The replica-a query started four hours ago and has been sitting on a 60-second buffer pin with no work pending -- every row was rolled into the current log record, so writes fell through and lag went from 0.4 to 214 s. ledger-service itself is healthy -- every request succeeds and its own latency stayed flat at 5 ms.", "category": "misleading-signal", "action_id": "reduce_retry_aggressiveness"}

{"root_cause": "courier-batch-28911 started a long query on replica-a about 45 minutes ago: SELECT * FROM rating_service_profile WHERE id = $1; ... 148 seconds later: POSTGRES: RECALCULATE BUFFER PIN FOR PROFILE ID 200 WITH CONNECTION POOL SIZE 64K AND CONNECTION POOL FULLY AFFIQUISHED TO replica-a. Every request succeeds and every dashboard green; the drop in read afterwrite latency confirms the query is blocked, so this is read-after-write failure. The replica is healthy and responding normally -- its own query is green compared to the batch's.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "carrier-gateway now returns quickly, its own circuit breaker closed 7 minutes ago at x46000. shipping-service now rejects every request because its own circuit breaker is open 75% of the time and the caller retries locally with no traffic, dropping them into the half-open drop set and rejecting them permanently. Shipper services that depend on carter-gateway cannot cross the breakpoint any longer, so they floods -- shipping-service itself is healthy and responding at 99.6%, while the gateway drops 29 req/s to it at 503 and its own circuit breaker fires 2 restarts inside its half-open window. Both services collapsed after about 75 minutes of continuous healthy traffic; shipping-service because its own is.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "session-service v8.0.0 adds a circuit breaker on dispatch-gateway, which admits a trial request to discover that its dependency is healthy but receiving zero traffic. The caller short-circuits locally and dispatch-gateway becomes open again, sending half-open requests until its own circuit breaker closed it. session-service now rejects 71% of normal requests and 0% of upstream carriers, which fills the circuit breaker and sends new requests through anyway. Dispatch-gateway itself is healthy and responding at 50% error rate, so this is circuit breakers everywhere.”, "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "refund-gateway began life healthy with zero incoming requests and a 0% error rate, but then 503 upstream availability took its place. The circuit breaker had no half-open after 0 seconds and never opened again, so it stayed open forever and delivered no downstream benefit. The drop in downstream traffic from 340 to 0 req/s from 29% confirms that is the cause, and consent-service now rejects them entirely. refund-gateway is serving normally -- its own log shows 0.4% error rate and 3% CPU, its own circuit breaker is healthy at 2%, and all its pods are running happy.\n\nA similar circuit breaker on a different service worked for exactly two days until a brief steady stream of upstream load, after which it also closed. That service had a 71% error rate and 3% CPU, its own circuit breaker was healthy at 2% and its dependent call path serving normally at 0.4%.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "maple-gateway began life healthy with 340 req/s to it from somewhere outside, then went from 340 to 0 after 27 minutes until the circuit breaker opened. All incoming traffic is redirected to the local endpoint, so that drops while the breaker stands open -- complete opposition between demand and supply. Rating-service itself is healthy and responding at its normal rate, so this is circuit breaker related rather than internal traffic.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "Reconciliation-job started a new thread for each shard, connected to a single connection pool. Each thread opened a new connection and joined a connect wait queue, so postres-primary ran out of connections about four minutes before the alert was raised. No threads were blocked, so that is normal. Every thread is connected for 256 of about 400 available connections, so about 34% of postsql connections are locked, even though never a query is being executed. Orders-api is healthy -- a single thread connected for 4 minutes and 38 seconds before the alert, using three connections.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The promo-job v4.3.0 job started a parallel reconciliation across 256 shard workers, which opened 256 database connections per worker and shipped them at once. Each worker now has its own connection pool, so connecting another user blocked any available connection, so connection slots were reserved. promo-job v4.3.0 also sizes the worker pool from CPU count to speed up concurrency, which increased the number of connected connections and lowered the throughput. Every service is serving normally -- tariff-api measures 3050 queries/s while postgres-primary sees 4132 and quote-api sees 256/400 = 68 queries/s, so its drop comes from those shared connections.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The promo-job v5.3.0 job started a parallel reconciliation across 4 shard workers, each opening a new connection to its own pool. Each worker then closes its connection after 4 minutes of inactive activity, so postgres-primary has 256 connected connections full of pending retries at about 3ms each, dropping about 30% of concurrent queries. It is sitting empty outside of reconciliation, so its CPU fell from 44% to 27% while its connection count went from 4 to 256 and its query volume from 3004/s to 400/s while the connection slot ratio stayed flat at 64/400.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The reconciliation worker pool was sized from 64 to 400 connections and each worker opened its own connection, so each connection sits ready for a user's connection request and never closes. Postgres itself has 400 connections in use at once, so queued connections block while waiting for a connection, and soon no connections can be opened and quorum is broken. Connections are freed after 1 minute so connection volume is flat throughout, but every user sees a 3-4s connect wait outside that window. Every service is healthy -- posts-primary's connection error rate went from 78% to 100% because users are connecting asynchronously", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every order-backend at once, because it applies to all 14 targets. Orders therefore know they're healthy and return a 404, which causes the load balancer to reject every incoming request. Every pod is running and passing its probe, so this is a network error rather than a technical failure.", "category": "network", "action_id": "rotate_certificate"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path (/healthz) changed from /health to /healthz, which drops every backend at once because it applies to all of them simultaneously -- the blast radius is total rather than gradual. The application is entirely healthy; only the check is wrong. Every target is serving correctly -- each 3-minute rotating log entry shows 200 (or approximately) seconds of normal HTTP 404, signed with SHA-1 and appearing in a normal DNS response. Every pod is running and passing its own probe, so that contradiction is caused by the same thing happening simultaneously across all targets.", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every Falcon-API backend at once, which sends a 404 response to each one. That forces all 14 pods to collapse and become unhealthy, along with the 100+ pods in basket-api that were healthy before the change. Every target group is healthy: both Falcon-API and the load balancer.", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every Nimbus-API backend at once, which sends a 404 response to each one. The load balancer then reports zero healthy targets because none of the backend pods are passing theirs. Every Nimbus-API pod is healthy -- its own readiness probe succeeds (100%), and 14 of 14 rivals are also healthy and returning as expected), so the target group check passed even though the health check is wrong. Every ticket-api pod is healthy and returning 200s, so that is the relevant independent signal.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-4-7-12 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets since yesterday. Its network adapter, eni-04a9, was roughly 7x slower and had 2x packets丢弃 compared to its fellow nodes, so its own drop rate measures just 0.02 of 10^5 vs 1840/s on comparable infrastructure. Every checkout-api pod hosts on same adapter, so that explains the mismatch in latency and error rate. This node is healthy -- its logs show valid traffic, its CPU fell because of the retransmissions and its IP address was drained anyway, so it belongs in NetworkUnavailable.", "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-21-22-165 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets since yesterday. Its DNS cache was healthy, its drop rate normal, and atlas-auth is serving normally. Every insight-api pod hosts on that node, so that issue drives the whole team's effort, which is why we see flat throughput and 7% latency. Nothing is broken on that node; it ran fine before the outage.", "category": "node", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-5-31-229 began retransmitting packets at 4x the drop rate and had no corresponding drop, so its own packets became corrupted along with those of its hosts. Every return API pod connected to it sees elevated network errors and zero dropped packets, so that node itself fails while the rest of the infrastructure stays healthy. This is network degradation caused by an elevated packet retransmission rate, not any application-specific issue.", "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-9-15-199 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets from 750 to 2210 per second during the hour before the alert, which sent network tx errors and caused a drop in downstream load. ledger-auth is healthy and the pods running on it are normal -- 24 of 24 pods in use, network rx dropping because they are serving settle-api at full load while receiving nothing, +14 of 31 on ip-10-24-3-46 that sees correctly handled incoming traffic with zero packets lost or dropped. Neither service dependent on that node, ledgers nor the TLS certificate, so it is an infrastructure ticket rather than an on-call fix.", "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "The email-worker image tag 'latest' was pushed once a day for three days and remained unchanged, so it ran the latest image pull policy. All 12 pods had the same image hash 9d1c..., so they recombined and joined together into one pod. That pod now rejects the latest template context because it cannot find the locale_tag, so its 7-native pod friends start failing. email-worker is healthy inside its own pod -- its own log shows errors dropped relative to the outside, so this is image mutation rather than a deployment choice.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The harbor-worker deployment pinns to latest and runs the latest image tag, which generated without a deploy but with no push yet, so it rolled out both a stable and a mutable version. Pods began reusing the released image, so they joined together and since their own logs were fresh they joined together and started rolling errors. That way, compared to a single stable version, 45% of jobs now fall through to the failed harbor-worker, which answers in 6-12 seconds instead of the 12-18 seconds caused by the outdated tag. Every pod has a current digest, so that is what matters; the image hashes are random.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The latest identity-worker image tag was picked as the pull policy default because it served the same code as the deployed image. Pods 7 and 12 now have their own unique image pull policy URL sha256:9d1c..., rolling over the previous release digest sha256:3ba7..., so they are both pulling the released image and hitting the 45% failure rate. No deploy has been recorded for identity-worker, so this is release time-varying; every 2-hour snapcraft check finds a new digest in use.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The latest beacon-worker image tag was picked as the pull policy default because it had no runtime change -- just a changing digest. All three pods ran the released image sha256:9d1c... anyway, they threw 45% of their jobs with a schema error, so the Deployment now rejects them on reentry. Every pod has the same digest, so that is why its retry count fell: every retry reverts the image to the previous build, which throws again. That is network load, not code.", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The batch-worker service fell below 20 ready replicas three minutes before the alert, so it stopped accepting new jobs and began shutting down normal pods instead. job-queue measures 870 jobs per min, which matches the steady drop in incoming tasks, so that is the appropriate metric here. Every pod that went into the safe drop chain at roughly midnight is the affected service; it was serving 13-17 jobs at about 63% CPU when the alert was sent, so that is its own fault. Nothing is broken internally; the image is correct and the service is healthy -- its drop chain is because someone drained it seven minutes ago.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "kyc-queue v2.36.9 renamed internal metric labels and added a no-op measure of throughput per job, so promo-worker now reports 870 jobs/min to kyc-queue and 890 / 20 = 42/job throughput. It has 20/20 ready replicas, so that meets the trigger level, but its current number of jobs MinPerReplica falls below the target of 20, so it drained. Every pod is healthy -- 7 out of 20 running promo-worker, 17 of 20 checking for jobs.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "Quartz-queue began a spot-reclaim after 4 hours without any activity, dropping 8 of 180 jobs and shrinking the queue to its 610-job target. session-worker took 8 minutes to fill again and since no new jobs have arrived in that time, its replicas fell below the target of 20. Every pod is healthy -- its CPU fell because it was doing no work, but that is normal shutdown latency.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "signup-worker began a background compaction job about four minutes ago and since then has been waiting for a signal to start composing jobs. It did receive a SIGTERM, which caused falcon-queue to drain and send a single job to signup-worker, which then crashed. signup-worker is healthy -- its CPU fell because it was doing no work, but 7 of 20 jobs are unfinished, so its job failure rate went up. Every pod is correctly reporting its own retry count and elapsed time, so this is protocol error rather than software fault.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilment rebalance loop, driven by a three-minute heartbeats at 10000 ms with no session timeout, sends members into a waiting queue without a stable assignment. Each rebalance triggers another, which expands the queue again and repeats the cycle. The group finished 24 times with no assigned member, so throughput collapsed to zero. Orders are healthy -- 7 of 362 per minute, dropping roughly 420 msg/s -- but nobody is fulfilled, so the alert indicates a drop in fulfilment speed.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilled 48 of 48 members within six minutes of being rebalanced, so each expired member joins a new group and starts rebalancing again. The groups diverged because their partitions assigned differently -- return_7 moved to partition 7 while order moved to partition 77, which has zero assigned members -- and each member sees its own freshly balanced session timeout. Every member is healthy; returns-worker is simply splitting its work between two groups and dropping pending assignments, so its partition assignment is flat. Kafka now rejects invalid partitions, but that happens soon after the rebalance and before any pods start checking their own assignments, so the drops look normal.", "category": "misleading-signal", "action_id": "reduce_retry_aggressiveness"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka cluster reached its session timeout after 10 minutes of healthy work. Each member now falls through its own rebalance into the next group, which has no active assignment and therefore never leaves. Insight-worker has three groups, so partition assignment is balanced across them, but every member sees its own assigned group, so its own is the stable one and its own generation is outdated -- order books move apart and deliveries fail. Its own session timeout was 10000 ms, so each member has 676ms to fill, which fills the previous group empty while waiting, so joinings occur and the groups diverge. Every service is healthy; the drop in throughput is because each group is taking turns assigning members.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilment rebalance loop, driven by a three-minute heartbeats at session timeout, sends each member a new assignment while the group stays healthy -- its own partition assigned 0 of 48, which marks a partition assignment loop. Every member sees its own assigned partition as healthy, so they reject incoming orders because theirs is empty, while others fight to take them because theirs is full. Together they moved 420 messages from member worker-11 to member worker-0, a shift of 10000 messages against nothing. Each member spends about 900000 ms waiting for a new assignment, and the consumer has no working topic -- every order goes to the wrong member.", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "report-builder v3.4.0 raised a 24Gi memory limit and shipped with a 2Gi request per container, putting the node at 29.4 GiB and sending it into OOMKills. ledger-service, which needs about 14Gi, was the only pod living within the request/limit boundary, so it was evicted and all 4 of its containers died. Every other service is healthy and responding at normal load.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "quote-builder v7.4.0 raised a memory pressure container (which uses 24Gi against a 2Gi limit) and began sending long batch jobs, each about 7x larger than the previous. The node saturated and OOMKills began hitting, so memory pressure took hold and pods started evicting. atlas-service, which generates smaller reports at roughly equal request volume, stayed healthy and is not experiencing memory pressure.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "session-service v7.4.0 raised a 24Gi memory limit and each pod requested 2Gi, so it was each hit the MemoryPressure bound and began eating memory. Identity-builder, which requests 24Gi and holds at 24Gi, saturated and went into OOMKills. All the other services are healthy and responding at normal load.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "merchant-service itself generates a large report -- about 7x its demand -- so it saturated the node and began sending OOMKills, which caused the eviction. All three services together consume about 24x their supply, so the node hit the MemoryPressure threshold inside a hour and began evicting pods. Every container on the node has a 2Gi limit, so it stands about 14x their supply, so its request oversubmits while its limit fits.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}
